claim: MN1-GAL4 expresses selectively in a pair of segmentally repeated motoneurons that form synapses onto muscle 1 of the dorsal body wall.
source: The GAL4 line MN1-GAL4 (previously referred to as MN1-Ib-GAL4; Kim et al., 2009) expresses selectively in a pair of segmentally repeated motoneurons that form synapses onto muscle 1 of the dorsal body wall (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2009 and reference to Figure 1A showing the expression pattern.

claim: UAS-Shal-RNAi completely eliminates Shal protein when driven pan-neuronally.
source: We combined MN1-GAL4 with a previously described UAS-Shal-RNAi that was shown to completely eliminate Shal protein when driven pan-neuronally (Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: Shal-RNAi driven by MN1-GAL4 causes a dramatic reduction in somatically measured IKA.
source: Consistent with the previously documented effectiveness of the Shal-RNAi transgene, we found a dramatic reduction in somatically measured IKA when Shal-RNAi was driven by MN1-GAL4 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In wild-type MN1, IKA activated at approximately −30 mV and reached an average current density of 20 pA/pF at +40 mV.
source: In wild-type MN1, IKA activated at approximately −30 mV and reached an average current density of 20 pA/pF at +40 mV.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements reported in the text.

claim: In MN1 expressing Shal-RNAi, no substantial current was present until +20 mV, and voltage steps above +20 mV revealed only a small outward current with IKA characteristics.
source: By contrast, no substantial current was present in MN1 expressing Shal-RNAi until +20 mV, and voltage steps above +20 mV revealed only a small outward current with IKA characteristics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements reported in the text.

claim: The Shal495 protein null mutation demonstrates a +50 mV shift in voltage activation.
source: Importantly, prior characterization of a Shal protein null mutation demonstrated the same current-voltage trajectory, including the same observed +50 mV shift in voltage activation (Bergquist et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bergquist et al., 2010.

claim: The remaining voltage-shifted outward current in Shal null mutants reflects homeostatic upregulation of the Shaker channel.
source: In that prior study, the remaining, voltage-shifted, outward current was determined to reflect the homeostatic upregulation of the Shaker channel, which resides in the electrotonically distant axonal membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study (Bergquist et al., 2010).

claim: Shaker channels are localized at an electrotonically distant site in the axon and presynaptic terminal.
source: We can rule out a major contribution of Shaker to the 4-AP effect because Shaker channels are localized at an electrotonically distant site in the axon and presynaptic terminal (Ford and Davis, 2014); Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ford and Davis, 2014 and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Shal-RNAi effectively eliminated the relevant somatic IKA that would participate in action potential repolarization.
source: Given these data, we conclude that Shal-RNAi effectively eliminated the relevant somatic IKA that would participate in action potential repolarization.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and prior studies cited.

claim: Acute application of 4-AP caused a significant increase in MN1 firing rate compared to wild type across all current steps greater than 50 pA.
source: We demonstrate that application of 4-AP caused a significant increase in MN1 firing rate compared to wild type across all current steps greater than 50 pA (Figure 1C & D; WT + 4 AP, orange traces).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: At current steps above 150 pA with 4-AP application, depolarization block was routinely observed.
source: At current steps above 150 pA, depolarization block was routinely observed, limiting the maximal firing rate that could be quantified (Figure 1C, arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Depolarization block was never observed in wild type.
source: Depolarization block was never observed in wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations reported in the text.

claim: Shal knockdown in MN1 did not result in a significant change in firing rate.
source: By contrast, Shal knockdown in MN1, eliminating somatic IKA (Figure 1B), did not result in a significant change in firing rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and firing rate measurements.

claim: Depolarization block was never observed following Shal knockdown, just as in wild type.
source: Furthermore, depolarization block was never observed, just as in wild type (Figure 1C & D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: 4-AP does not alter firing rate when applied to motoneurons lacking the Shal conductance.
source: Notably, 4-AP does not alter firing rate when applied to motoneurons lacking the Shal conductance, demonstrating the specificity of 4-AP at the concentration used in these experiments (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data referenced in the text.

claim: FRH can be induced and expressed in a single neuron.
source: Based on this argument, we provide evidence that FRH can be induced and expressed in a single neuron.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing cell-autonomous firing rate homeostasis.

claim: Acute application of 4-AP caused a significant reduction in the after-hyperpolarization amplitude with no significant effect on amplitude or half-width.
source: Acute application of 4-AP caused a significant reduction in the after-hyperpolarization amplitude with no significant effect on amplitude or half-width (AHP, AP amp. and AP HW, respectively; Figure 1E & F; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1) for how these measurements are made).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: No significant changes in action potential waveform were observed when somatic IKA was eliminated selectively in MN1.
source: By contrast, no significant changes were observed when somatic IKA was eliminated selectively in MN1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of action potential waveform parameters.

claim: The half-maximal effect of 4-AP on IKA in other systems is 1–2 mM and is considered to have reasonable specificity.
source: Furthermore, the half-maximal effect of 4-AP on IKA in other systems (1–2 mM) is considered to have reasonable specificity and this concentration of 4-AP has quantitatively similar effects in Drosophila (Ford and Davis, 2014; Jackson and Bean, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ford and Davis, 2014 and Jackson and Bean, 2007.

claim: Action potential repolarization and neuronal firing rate are statistically identical to wild type following the elimination of the Shal-mediated somato-dendritic IKA current.
source: Regardless, it is remarkable that action potential repolarization and neuronal firing rate are statistically identical to wild type following the elimination of the Shal-mediated somato-dendritic IKA current.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing wild type and Shal-RNAi conditions.

claim: Conservation of action potential waveform occurs despite the absence of a primary fast potassium channel conductance (IKA).
source: Thus, we demonstrate conservation of action potential waveform despite the absence of a primary fast potassium channel conductance (IKA).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing preserved action potential waveform.

claim: The W362F point mutation in the Shal channel pore is a highly conserved mutation demonstrated to function as a pore-blocking mutation in mammalian heterologous cells and cultured Drosophila embryonic neurons.
source: This point mutation is a single amino acid substitution in the channel pore (W362F), a highly conserved mutation demonstrated to function as a pore-blocking mutation in systems as diverse as mammalian heterologous cells and cultured Drosophila embryonic neurons (Barry et al., 1998; Ping et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barry et al., 1998 and Ping et al., 2011.

claim: Overexpression of the pore-blocked Shal channel traffics to the plasma membrane both in vitro and in vivo.
source: We note that, both in vitro and in vivo, overexpression of this pore-blocked channel traffics to the plasma membrane (Barry et al., 1998; Ping et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barry et al., 1998 and Ping et al., 2011.

claim: Motoneurons in the homozygous ShalW362F mutant lack somatically recorded IKA.
source: Here, we demonstrate that motoneurons in the homozygous ShalW362F mutant lack somatically recorded IKA (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Robust FRH exists in ShalW362F and is just as precise as that observed when Shal was eliminated using UAS-Shal-RNAi expressed in MN1.
source: Next, we demonstrate the existence of robust FRH in ShalW362F, and it is just as precise as that observed when Shal was eliminated using UAS-Shal-RNAi expressed in MN1 (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Bath application of 4-AP did not increase firing rates in ShalW362F mutant neurons.
source: In contrast to wild-type motoneurons, bath application of 4-AP did not increase firing rates in ShalW362F mutant neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: FRH can be induced by the loss of Shal channel function as well as loss of Shal protein.
source: Thus, FRH can be induced by the loss of Shal channel function as well as loss of Shal protein.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results comparing Shal-RNAi and ShalW362F.

claim: FRH is achieved by compensatory changes in ion channel gene expression.
source: We hypothesized, based on work in Drosophila and other systems, that FRH is achieved by compensatory changes in ion channel gene expression (Marder and Prinz, 2002; Nerbonne et al., 2008; Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marder and Prinz, 2002; Nerbonne et al., 2008; and Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: A significant enhancement of IKDR and IKCa was found in MN1 lacking Shal compared to wild type.
source: We found a significant enhancement of IKDR and IKCa, but no change in sodium or calcium currents in MN1 lacking Shal compared to wild type (Figure 2A,B,C & D, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: No change in sodium or calcium currents was found in MN1 lacking Shal compared to wild type.
source: We found a significant enhancement of IKDR and IKCa, but no change in sodium or calcium currents in MN1 lacking Shal compared to wild type (Figure 2A,B,C & D, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The IKCa current was virtually eliminated in the slo mutant.
source: The IKCa current was virtually eliminated in the slo mutant (Figure 2B, gray line).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both BK and SK channel transcripts are increased in the Shal495 null mutant background.
source: We previously demonstrated that both BK and SK channel transcripts are increased in the Shal495 null mutant background (Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: The elevated IKCa in the Shal-RNAi background is primarily due to an increase in Slo-dependent IKCa.
source: While we cannot rule out a contribution of SK channels, we propose that the elevated IKCa in the Shal-RNAi background is primarily due to an increase in Slo-dependent IKCa (see also below).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and prior observations.

claim: A significant change in the delayed rectifier current (IKDR) was observed in MN1 expressing Shal-RNAi.
source: We also observed a significant change in the delayed rectifier current (IKDR) in MN1 expressing Shal-RNAi (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Changes in IKDR in Kv4.2 knockout cardiac myocytes and pyramidal neurons in mice parallel the changes observed in Drosophila.
source: This effect parallels similar changes in IKDR in Kv4.2 knockout cardiac myocytes (Guo et al., 2005) and pyramidal neurons in mice (Nerbonne et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2005 and Nerbonne et al., 2008.

claim: The IKDR current can be encoded by four genes in Drosophila including: Shab, Shaw, Shawl and KCNQ.
source: The IKDR current can be encoded by four genes in Drosophila including: Shab, Shaw, Shawl and KCNQ.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila ion channel genes.

claim: XE991 is a potent and selective inhibitor of KCNQ channels in both mammals and Drosophila.
source: However, the drug XE991 is a potent and selective inhibitor of KCNQ channels in both mammals and Drosophila (Cavaliere and Hodge, 2011; Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cavaliere and Hodge, 2011 and Wang et al., 1998.

claim: Application of XE991 (10 µM) diminished IKDR in wild type MN1, but there was no differential effect following Shal-RNAi.
source: Application of XE991 (10 µM) diminished IKDR in wild type MN1, but there was no differential effect following Shal-RNAi (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data mentioned in the text.

claim: Expression of the Krüppel (Kr) transcription factor is induced by genetic depletion or pharmacological inhibition of the Shal channel.
source: We previously demonstrated that expression of the Krüppel (Kr) transcription factor is induced by genetic depletion or pharmacological inhibition of the Shal channel (Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: Kr expression is virtually absent in the wild type third instar CNS, but becomes highly expressed following loss of Shal.
source: Kr expression is virtually absent in the wild type third instar CNS, but becomes highly expressed following loss of Shal (Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: Over-expression of Kr in post-mitotic neurons is sufficient to drive changes in ion channel gene expression.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of Kr in post-mitotic neurons is sufficient to drive changes in ion channel gene expression (Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: When Kr and Shal are simultaneously knocked down in MN1, firing rates were significantly decreased compared to wild type at all current steps above 25 pA.
source: However, when Kr and Shal are simultaneously knocked down in MN1, firing rates were significantly decreased compared to wild type at all current steps above 25 pA (Figure 3A & B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Induction of Kr expression following loss of Shal is required for FRH.
source: These data are consistent with the conclusion that induction of Kr expression following loss of Shal is required for FRH.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing impaired FRH when Kr is knocked down.

claim: Firing rates are equivalent when comparing wild type and MN1-GAL4 > Shal RNAi animals.
source: Firing rates are equivalent when comparing wild type and MN1-GAL4 > Shal RNAi animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Firing rates are unchanged when comparing wild type and MN1-GAL4 > Kr RNAi animals.
source: Firing rates are also unchanged when comparing wild type and MN1-GAL4 > Kr RNAi animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Post mitotic knockdown of Kr has no baseline effect on firing rates.
source: This is an important control, demonstrating that post mitotic knockdown of Kr, a master regulator of cell fate in the embryo, has no baseline effect.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing no change in firing rates with Kr-RNAi alone.

claim: In the Shal-RNAi condition, action potential (AP) waveforms are indistinguishable from wild type.
source: In the Shal-RNAi condition, action potential (AP) waveforms are indistinguishable from wild type, arguing for preservation of AP waveform during FRH (Figure 3C,D & E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D, and E.

claim: Kr-RNAi has no effect on AP waveform.
source: We found that Kr-RNAi has no effect on AP waveform.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of action potential waveform parameters.

claim: When Shal and Kr were simultaneously knocked down in MN1, AP waveforms were significantly altered.
source: However, when Shal and Kr were simultaneously knocked down in MN1, AP waveforms were significantly altered (Figure 3C & D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The after-hyperpolarization amplitude was significantly smaller and AP half-width duration was significantly increased in double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi compared to wild type.
source: Specifically, the after-hyperpolarization amplitude was significantly smaller and AP half-width duration was significantly increased compared to wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of action potential waveform parameters.

claim: Kr participates in homeostatic control of both action potential waveform and firing rates following loss of Shal.
source: Thus, Kr participates in homeostatic control of both action potential waveform and firing rates following loss of Shal.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing altered AP waveform and firing rates when Kr is knocked down.

claim: Kr is a master regulator of cell fate determination in neurons.
source: It is well established that Kr is a master regulator of cell fate determination in neurons (Isshiki et al., 2001) and other cell types (McConnell and Yang, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Isshiki et al., 2001 and McConnell and Yang, 2010.

claim: There was no change in MN1 cell number or gross morphology in the CNS across the four genotypes examined.
source: There was no change in MN1 cell number or gross morphology in the CNS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B,C & D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: No significant differences in somatic diameter and proximal dendrite width were observed across the four genotypes.
source: We further measured somatic diameter and the width of the proximal dendrite as features that contribute to the passive electrical properties of these cells. No significant differences were observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E & F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: A decrease in input resistance was found for both Kr-RNAi and combined Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi.
source: Finally, we quantified cell capacitance and input resistance (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G & H). We found a decrease in input resistance for both Kr-RNAi and combined Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H.

claim: The double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition had the highest variability of all four genotypes for current steps above 100 pA.
source: The double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition had the highest variability of all four genotypes, an effect that is not additive for current steps above 100 pA.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of coefficient of variation across cells.

claim: No individual cell in the double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition ever fired at rates exceeding wild type.
source: Finally, it is worth noting that no individual cell ever fired at rates exceeding wild type as we observe following application of 4-AP (Figure 1D), indicating that the loss of firing rate homeostasis is not without some remaining constraint on firing frequencies in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations comparing individual cell firing rates.

claim: The increase in IKCa following loss of Shal was completely blocked by simultaneous Kr knockdown.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the increase in IKCa following loss of Shal was completely blocked by simultaneous Kr knockdown (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Kr knockdown had no effect on baseline IKCa.
source: Importantly, Kr knockdown had no effect on baseline IKCa (Figure 5D) or on voltage-gated calcium currents in the Shal-RNAi background (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Kr knockdown had no effect on voltage-gated calcium currents in the Shal-RNAi background.
source: Importantly, Kr knockdown had no effect on baseline IKCa (Figure 5D) or on voltage-gated calcium currents in the Shal-RNAi background (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Kr is required for the homeostatic enhancement of IKCa.
source: Thus, Kr is required for the homeostatic enhancement of IKCa.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing blocked IKCa enhancement when Kr is knocked down.

claim: Kr is the first gene demonstrated to have a selective action for homeostatic changes in channel function, without altering baseline channel activity.
source: To our knowledge, Kr is the first gene demonstrated to have a selective action for homeostatic changes in channel function, without altering baseline channel activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing Kr's specific role in homeostatic regulation.

claim: IKDR remained elevated in the double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition, similar to that observed in Shal-RNAi alone.
source: Next, we examined IKDR. We found that IKDR remained elevated in the double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition (Figure 5A), similar to that observed in Shal-RNAi alone (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and comparison to Figure 2A.

claim: Kr does not control the homeostatic upregulation of IKDR following loss of Shal.
source: This suggests that Kr does not control the homeostatic upregulation of IKDR following loss of Shal.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing maintained IKDR elevation without Kr.

claim: Kr knockdown alone had no effect on baseline IKDR.
source: We confirmed that Kr knockdown alone had no effect on baseline IKDR (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IKA was knocked down just as efficiently in double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi neurons as when Shal-RNAi was driven alone.
source: Finally, as another control, we quantified IKA in double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi neurons and demonstrate that IKA was knocked down just as efficiently as when Shal-RNAi was driven alone (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Loss of Kr participates in a specific facet of FRH induced by loss of Shal.
source: Thus, we conclude that loss of Kr participates in a specific facet of FRH induced by loss of Shal.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing Kr's selective control of IKCa.

claim: Bath application of paxilline (600 nM) to both wild-type and Shal-RNAi preparations significantly reduced firing rates in MN1.
source: We bath applied the selective BK channel inhibitor paxilline (600 nM) to both wild-type and Shal-RNAi preparations, and observed significantly reduced firing rates in MN1 (Figure 6A,B & C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, B, and C.

claim: Paxilline reduced maximal firing rates by 34% on average.
source: Paxilline reduced maximal firing rates by 34% on average, compared to the 12% reduction due to driving Kr-RNAi in the Shal-RNAi background.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of firing rates with paxilline application.

claim: Driving Kr-RNAi in the Shal-RNAi background reduced maximal firing rates by 12%.
source: Paxilline reduced maximal firing rates by 34% on average, compared to the 12% reduction due to driving Kr-RNAi in the Shal-RNAi background.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of firing rates in the double RNAi condition.

claim: Paxilline application resulted in decreased AHP amplitude and a larger AP half-width duration.
source: The effects of paxilline on action potential waveform were also consistent with those seen in the double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition. We observed decreased AHP amplitude and a larger AP half-width duration (Figure 5D & E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Loss of Slo-dependent AP repolarization leads to a broader action potential and shallower AHP, which impedes recovery of sodium channels from inactivation and causes decreased firing rate.
source: Loss of Slo-dependent AP repolarization leads to the observed broader action potential and shallower AHP, an effect that is predicted to impede recovery of sodium channels from inactivation and thus cause decreased firing rate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results and known biophysical properties of sodium channels.

claim: Upregulation of IKDR occurs in ShalW362F.
source: First, we demonstrate upregulation of IKDR in ShalW362F (Figure 7A), consistent with this expectation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No significant change in IKCa was found in ShalW362F.
source: Furthermore, we found no significant change in IKCa (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Slo transcript is upregulated following loss of Shal protein.
source: We confirmed, via quantitative PCR, that Slo transcript is upregulated following loss of Shal protein (Figure 7E; see Parrish et al., 2014 for initial observation).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7E and citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: No change in Slo transcript was observed in the ShalW362F non-conducting mutant.
source: However, we did not observe a change in Slo transcript in the ShalW362F non-conducting mutant (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A small but statistically significant broadening of the AP waveform was observed in ShalW362F.
source: In agreement, we observed a small but statistically significant broadening of the AP waveform in ShalW362F (Figure 7C & D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: FRH appears to be differentially achieved in ShalW362F compared to Shal-RNAi.
source: Thus, FRH appears to be differentially achieved in ShalW362F compared to Shal-RNAi.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing different compensatory mechanisms.

claim: The transcripts for Krüppel, Shaker, slo, and Shab are significantly elevated in the shal null mutant (Shal495).
source: The transcripts for all four of these genes are significantly elevated in the shal null mutant (Shal495; Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: The transcription of Krüppel, Shaker, slo, and Shab was increased in the Shal null mutant.
source: Confirming prior observations using gene expression arrays (Parrish et al., 2014), the transcription all four genes was increased in the Shal null mutant (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7E and citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: None of the genes Krüppel, Shaker, slo, and Shab showed altered expression in ShalW362F.
source: However, none of these genes showed altered expression in ShalW362F (Figure 7F, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: There was no change in the expression of KCNQ, Shaw and Shawl in ShalW362F.
source: We then extended this analysis in ShalW362F to include KCNQ, Shaw and Shawl (Figure 7F, top). Again, there was no change in the expression of these channels, whereas KCNQ was upregulated in the Shal null (Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F and citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: KCNQ was upregulated in the Shal null.
source: Again, there was no change in the expression of these channels, whereas KCNQ was upregulated in the Shal null (Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claim: All wild-type and ShalW362F flies climbed up the walls of a glass vial above 10 cm within 10 s.
source: All wild-type and ShalW362F flies climbed up the walls of a glass vial above 10 cm within 10 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: No statistically significant differences in average climbing speed were detected between wild-type and ShalW362F flies.
source: No statistically significant differences in average climbing speed were detected, consistent with the idea that FRH enables normal motor behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: Pan-neuronal Shal knockdown (elav-Gal4; Shal-RNAi) dramatically altered animal behavior, and every animal tested failed to ascend past the 10 cm mark within 30 s.
source: Instead, pan-neuronal Shal knockdown dramatically altered animal behavior, and every animal that was tested failed to ascend past the 10 cm mark within 30 s, the maximal allotted time.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: Control animals (Shal-RNAi/+) were no different from wild type in climbing behavior.
source: Control animals (Shal-RNAi/+) were no different from wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: Motoneuron-specific Shal knockdown (OK371-Gal4) resulted in wild type climbing behavior.
source: As a further control, we assessed motoneuron-specific Shal knockdown (OK371-Gal4). In this experiment, climbing behavior was wild type, again consistent with the conclusion that FRH, which we demonstrate in motoneurons, is sufficient to restore normal animal behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: FRH induced by pan-neuronal knockdown of Shal interferes with the subsequent induction of presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) at the neuromuscular junction.
source: We previously demonstrated that FRH, induced by pan-neuronal knockdown of Shal, interferes with the subsequent induction of presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP), assayed at the neuromuscular junction (Bergquist et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bergquist et al., 2010.

claim: Increased Shaker expression blocks the expression of PHP that is selectively induced at the NMJ.
source: A current model for this interference effect is that increased Shaker expression, caused by the presence of the protein null Shal495 mutation or by direct over-expression of a Shaker transgene, blocks the expression of PHP that is selectively induced at the NMJ (Figure 7I & J; Bergquist et al., 2010; Parrish et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bergquist et al., 2010 and Parrish et al., 2014, and reference to Figure 7I and J.

claim: Increased levels of Shaker channel prevent ENaC channel-dependent depolarization of the presynaptic plasma membrane, which is necessary to increase presynaptic calcium influx that drives enhanced neurotransmitter release during PHP.
source: Increased levels of Shaker channel, which localizes to the presynaptic terminal at the NMJ (Figure 7), prevents ENaC channel-dependent depolarization of the presynaptic plasma membrane, which is necessary to increase presynaptic calcium influx that drives enhanced neurotransmitter release during PHP (Younger et al., 2013; Parrish et al., 2014; Orr et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Younger et al., 2013; Parrish et al., 2014; and Orr et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 7.

claim: Synapses in the pore-blocking ShalW362F mutant were capable of undergoing PHP.
source: Decreased mEPSP amplitude was precisely offset by an increase in presynaptic release (quantal content, QC) that restored EPSP amplitudes to pre-PhTx amplitudes in both wild type and ShalW362F animals (Figure 7K & L). Thus, unlike in the protein null Shal495 mutant, synapses in the pore-blocking ShalW362F mutant were capable of undergoing PHP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K and L.

claim: FRH can be induced and fully expressed in single, genetically identified neurons.
source: First, we demonstrate that FRH can be induced and fully expressed in single, genetically identified neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing FRH in MN1.

claim: Changes in the activity of a single motoneuron are unlikely to dramatically alter the behavior of the larvae.
source: Since changes in the activity of a single motoneuron are unlikely to dramatically alter the behavior of the larvae, these data argue strongly for cell autonomous mechanisms that detect the presence of the ion channel perturbation and induce a corrective, homeostatic response.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental design and results.

claim: FRH functions to preserve the waveform of individual action potentials.
source: Second, we demonstrate that FRH functions to preserve the waveform of individual action potentials.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing preserved AP waveform.

claim: The transcription factor Krüppel is essential for FRH.
source: Third, we provide new evidence that the transcription factor Krüppel is essential for FRH, and selectively controls the homeostatic enhancement of IKCA, without altering the baseline ion channel current.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing impaired FRH when Kr is knocked down.

claim: Different mechanisms of FRH are induced depending upon how the Shal current is eliminated.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that different mechanisms of FRH are induced depending upon how the Shal current is eliminated, and these differential expression mechanisms can have perturbation-specific effects on animal behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results comparing Shal-RNAi and ShalW362F.

claim: Parallel homeostatic mechanisms exist that are responsive to differential disruption of the Shal gene.
source: We propose the existence of parallel homeostatic mechanisms, responsive to differential disruption of the Shal gene.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from the experimental results showing different compensatory responses.

claim: Altered activity cannot be the sole determinant of FRH.
source: First, altered activity cannot be the sole determinant of FRH. Two functionally identical manipulations that eliminate the Shal conductance, each predicted to have identical effects on neuronal excitability, lead to molecularly distinct homeostatic responses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results comparing Shal-RNAi and ShalW362F.

claim: Homeostatic signaling systems are sensitive to the type of mutation that affects an ion channel gene.
source: Second, homeostatic signaling systems are sensitive to the type of mutation that affects an ion channel gene.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing different responses to different Shal mutations.

claim: Separable proteostatic and activity-dependent homeostatic signaling systems potentially act in concert to achieve cell-type-specific and perturbation-specific FRH.
source: Finally, our data speak to experimental and theoretical studies arguing that the entire repertoire of ion channels encoded in the genome is accessible to the mechanisms of homeostatic feedback, with a very large combinatorial solution space (Marder and Prinz, 2002; O'Leary et al., 2014). Our data are consistent with the existence of separable proteostatic and activity-dependent homeostatic signaling systems, potentially acting in concert to achieve cell-type-specific and perturbation-specific FRH.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and inference from the experimental results and cited theoretical work.

claim: FRH has been widely documented within invertebrate neurons and neural circuits as well as the vertebrate spinal cord, cortical pyramidal neurons and cardiomyocytes.
source: FRH has been widely documented within invertebrate neurons (Turrigiano et al., 1994; Muraro et al., 2008; Driscoll et al., 2013) and neural circuits (Haedo and Golowasch, 2006) as well as the vertebrate spinal cord (Gonzalez-Islas et al., 2010), cortical pyramidal neurons (Andrásfalvy et al., 2008) and cardiomyocytes (Guo et al., 2005; Marrus and Nerbonne, 2008; Michael et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The mechanisms of FRH correct for the loss of the ion channel and precisely restore neuronal firing properties to normal, wild-type levels.
source: The mechanisms of FRH correct for the loss of the ion channel and precisely restore neuronal firing properties to normal, wild-type levels (Swensen and Bean, 2005; Muraro et al., 2008; Andrásfalvy et al., 2008; Nerbonne et al., 2008; Van Wart and Matthews, 2006; Bergquist et al., 2010; Parrish et al., 2014); see also: MacLean et al., 2003; Ping and Tsunoda, 2012; Driscoll et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Little is understood about the underlying molecular mechanisms of FRH.
source: To date, little is understood about the underlying molecular mechanisms (but see Parrish et al., 2014; Joseph and Turrigiano, 2017; Goold and Nicoll, 2010; Mee et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the field and citations to limited prior mechanistic studies.

claim: The existing repertoire of channels expressed by a neuron can be 'rebalanced' to correct for the deletion of an ion channel.
source: Instead, the existing repertoire of channels expressed by a neuron can be 'rebalanced' to correct for the deletion of an ion channel (Swensen and Bean, 2005; Muraro et al., 2008; Andrásfalvy et al., 2008; Nerbonne et al., 2008; Van Wart and Matthews, 2006; Bergquist et al., 2010; Parrish et al., 2014; Driscoll et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Different mixtures of ion channels can achieve similar firing properties in a neuron.
source: Theoretical work argues that different mixtures of ion channels can achieve similar firing properties in a neuron (Marder and Prinz, 2002; Marder and Goaillard, 2006; O'Leary et al., 2014; Golowasch, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: A pervasive theory argues that a single physiological variable, calcium, is detected and stabilized through regulatory feedback control of ion channel gene expression.
source: These observations have led to a pervasive and intuitively attractive theory that a single physiological variable, calcium, is detected and stabilized through regulatory feedback control of ion channel gene expression (O'Leary et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to O'Leary et al., 2014.

claim: There remain few direct tests of the hypothesis that calcium is the only intracellular variable sensed and controlled by homeostatic feedback.
source: Is calcium the only intracellular variable that is sensed and controlled by homeostatic feedback? There remain few direct tests of this hypothesis (Joseph and Turrigiano, 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the field and citation to Joseph and Turrigiano, 2017.

claim: Homeostatic signaling systems appear unable to counteract disease-relevant ion channel mutations, including those linked to epilepsy and autism.
source: Why are homeostatic signaling systems seemingly unable to counteract disease-relevant ion channel mutations, including those that have been linked to risk for diseases such as epilepsy and autism (Ben-Shalom et al., 2017; Klassen et al., 2011)?
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the literature and citations to Ben-Shalom et al., 2017 and Klassen et al., 2011.
